Read with the 7 to 9.30 p.m. fight on East Cemetery Hill in Howard's report, it points to an assembly in the early evening, but the passage does not say that.

weighing.summary: No source states when the council began: the start hour is a gap, bounded by two witnesses of the same council. every witness who sat in it says evening or night; Meade (1864) puts his call for the corps commanders after the battle had ceased and darkness had set in; Hancock says fighting on the right was in progress at twilight and again after the commanders had assembled (he dates the fighting, not the assembly); Gibbon says the sitting continued up to nearly 12 o'clock, with fighting on the right during a part of it; Haskell says it was after evening came on and lasted some two hours; Gibbon's testimony says several hours. The Park Service handbook alone has "at midnight", and read as the start it is contradicted by Gibbon (it is the end). The plan's 21:00 has no source. So the default is the window the witnesses allow, from dusk to nearly midnight, and each of the plan's values stays selectable.
weighing.who: Meade called the council and Gibbon, Hancock and Sedgwick sat in it: they are the best witnesses to its place in the evening, and none gives an hour. Haskell was Gibbon's aide. Pleasonton says he was away. The Park Service handbook (1954, 1962) is a modern summary that cites no source for "midnight". The hour 21:00 comes from a secondary book the plan names (SS2) that is not in the record.
weighing.when: Meade, Gibbon, Hancock and Sedgwick wrote or testified between March and April 1864, eight to nine months after the council, in answer to the charge that Meade had meant to retreat: rank 4 (official reports within two years). Haskell wrote within weeks or months (rank 5, a private letter, exact day unknown). Sickles wrote in 1886, Pleasonton in 1883, the Park Service in 1954 and 1962 (reminiscence or institutional). No writing of the night gives an hour: the minutes printed in the Official Records (p.74), in pencil and found among Meade's papers, are indorsed "held Thursday p. m., July 2" by the chief of staff and carry no hour.
weighing.where: All the main witnesses were in the room: Gibbon says it was not 10 feet square and that the corps commanders were close together. Haskell was at the house. Hancock and Gibbon came from the front and were summoned by a staff officer. Pleasonton was away. The Park Service author was not there.
weighing.how_knew: Meade by his own orders; Gibbon, Hancock, Sedgwick and Sykes as members. None read a clock; the hours are inferred from darkness, twilight and the length of the sitting. Gibbon's "nearly 12" is the only clock expression for the council and it is a hedge.
weighing.clock: Union side throughout (staff time of the Army of the Potomac). No witness names a clock. The reported 20-minute difference between the two armies' clocks is not applied and is only noted as an uncertainty of a quarter of an hour on the upper bound; it is not needed to reconcile any pair of values here.
weighing.independence: The Park Service texts of 1954 and 1962 are one line (one handbook in two editions). Gibbon's letter, his testimony and Haskell are counted as one line: Haskell was his aide and they shared the headquarters. Meade, Hancock, Sedgwick, Sykes and Howard are separate lines; the lower bound rests on Meade and Gibbon, the upper bound on Gibbon alone, so the end of the window is single-witness; the hedge "nearly" is kept.

source_panel_text: Evening of Jul 2, from dusk (sunset 19:32) to nearly midnight. Gibbon, who sat in it, says the council "continued up to nearly 12 o'clock"; Meade's sworn testimony puts the summons after darkness fell. No source gives the start hour, so the plan's 21:00 start, the Park Service's midnight and "late" stay listed, with 7 other values.

what_would_change_it: Not applicable to a start hour. The lower bound is the standing sunset of 19:32; it is a computed time, so the window is inferred, not documented. A better source would be a timed order, log or diary entry of the evening of 2 July at headquarters (Butterfield's or Meade's own, or an aide's), or a letter of a corps commander written that night.
